card.hook: Picture a 30-metre figure with arms stretched 28 metres wide, and you craning your neck at its feet like everyone else. Christ the Redeemer is one of those rare landmarks where the pose does all the work, so you barely need to try.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the statue on the platform. The phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the figure, tilt your phone up and keep it level so the arms don't lean.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x when you're close to the base, so the full height and the arm span fit in. Switch to 1x for the statue with the city behind it, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the face and hands.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the middle of the statue up with the centre vertical line, so the arms balance left and right.
card.best_time: Mornings are a good bet, because the statue faces east. Cloud can sit around the summit, so if the top is hidden, wait a bit and check again.
card.selfie_here: Climb to the top of the stairs that lead up to the statue's front, which a visitor tip calls the only practical way to get you and the statue in one shot. On your own, use the front camera at 0.5x with the statue over your shoulder. The stairs tip is a few years old, so check it still works when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand at the foot of the same stairs and shoot upwards while you wait at the top.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are banned at the statue, large bags aren't allowed on the viewing platform, and please don't climb barriers for a photo. It's a very safe area, but pickpockets can work the crowds, so keep your phone and pockets in mind.
card.challenge: Strike the pose: arms out wide, then get a friend to line you up under the big guy's outstretched hands.
card.good_to_know: The statue was designed by Paul Landowski with Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa and built between 1922 and 1931. It's reinforced concrete covered in soapstone. Wind and lightning mean regular repairs, so you might see scaffolding on some visits.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the statue on the platform. The phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the figure, tilt your phone up and keep it level so the arms don't lean.

card.hook: Most people photograph Copacabana from the sand, and it never quite fits. Walk to the fort at the end and the whole four-kilometre curve fits in one shot, with Sugarloaf sitting behind it.
card.stand_here: Stand at Forte de Copacabana, on the seaward parapet or the walk along the outer wall at the south end of the beach by Posto 6. From the middle of the beach, the fort is about 2.3 km away, roughly a half-hour walk along the seafront, heading south. Face north and look back along the sand towards Leme.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole crescent of sand. Then take a calmer shot at 1x, and a third at 2x or more to pull Sugarloaf in closer (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and run the curve of the shoreline along a diagonal, with a bit of the parapet in the corner for depth.
card.best_time: Go early on a weekday or in late afternoon, when you get more room and softer light, and Sugarloaf looks its best. At Posto 6 you can also try a sunrise shot over the Atlantic.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the upper parapet of Forte de Copacabana at the southern tip, where the length of the beach stretches away behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the beach and Sugarloaf sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the Avenida Atlântica pavement, stand on the avenue side across from the Copacabana Palace and ask a passer-by to frame you so the white Art Deco facade fills the picture, with the beach just across the street.
card.rules_and_safety: Forte de Copacabana is a working army site with an entry fee, so bring photo ID and some cash, and check access before you set off. Photography is generally allowed in most areas, but respect any posted signs. At night, keep your phone out of sight on quieter streets.
card.challenge: Find the black-and-white wave pavement and use it as a line that leads the eye into your photo, then see how many umbrellas you can fit along it.
card.good_to_know: The wave-pattern promenade dates from the 1930s, was rebuilt in 1970, and was designed by Roberto Burle Marx. Fort Copacabana was built in 1914, and Fort Duque de Caxias at the other end goes back to 1779. On New Year's Eve an estimated two million people fill the beach for the fireworks.

card.hook: Most people ride up Sugarloaf to look at Rio. Here you do the opposite: you stand on the sand and look up at a 396 m granite giant rising straight out of the water. Craning your neck is part of the fun.
card.stand_here: Head for Praia Vermelha, the beach at the south-west base of Sugarloaf, and stand right at the subject on the sand. Face north-east and the mountain rises straight above you.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to try to squeeze in the rock, the bay and the green hillside, then go to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look. When the cable car glides by, try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick it out against the granite.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the sand or water in the bottom third and let the peak rise above it, keeping the phone level so the sides don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, about 9am to 11am, when guides say the light falls on the east face. For a sunset instead, try Mureta da Urca, where Sugarloaf sits behind the wall.
card.selfie_here: Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x and tuck the big rock over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little low so you and the peak both fit.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are restricted around here, so leave yours at home. The cable car and summit are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for the cable car to cross the sky, then catch it with the whole rock in the frame. Take a Live Photo so you can pick the best moment afterwards.
card.good_to_know: The Portuguese named Sugarloaf in the 16th century because it looked like the cone-shaped moulds used to carry blocks of refined sugar on ships. The cable car opened in 1912 and was the first in Brazil. The mountain is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, declared in 2012.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Praia Vermelha, the beach at the south-west base of Sugarloaf, and stand right at the subject on the sand. Face north-east and the mountain rises straight above you.

card.hook: Picture a huge curve of sand, a line of surfers bobbing in the waves, and two pointy peaks standing guard at the far end. At Ipanema you get all of it in one frame, and the best seat is on the rocks.
card.stand_here: Head for the Arpoador rocks, about 1.6 km along the shore from the middle of the beach, heading south-east. Stand on the rocks at the Arpoador point and look back along the sand towards the Dois Irmãos peaks.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the beach, the sky and the peaks into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer view along the sand, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out surfers or pull the mountains closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line, not the middle, then keep a rock or a surfer in the foreground for depth.
card.best_time: Sunset is the classic time here. Get there about 45 minutes early to grab a spot on the rocks, because they fill up fast, especially at weekends.
card.selfie_here: Climb to the top of the Arpoador rocks (Pedra do Arpoador) and turn around. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold it a little low, and the whole beach stretches out behind you toward Leblon.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and pose on the wave-pattern mosaic sidewalk beside the sand at Posto 9, so the beach and sea fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: A visitor review warns of petty theft on Ipanema Beach, so keep your phone close while you pose. Check current conditions before you go.
card.challenge: Find a lifeguard tower number on the sand and get it in your shot with a surfer in the water behind it. Bonus points if the surfer doesn't wipe out.
card.good_to_know: Ipanema became world famous through the bossa nova song "The Girl from Ipanema", written in 1962 by Antônio Carlos Jobim and Vinícius de Moraes. The pavement along the shore has mosaic patterns designed by Roberto Burle Marx, which make a fun low, graphic shot. In winter the waves can reach about three metres.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Arpoador rocks, about 1.6 km along the shore from the middle of the beach, heading south-east. Stand on the rocks at the Arpoador point and look back along the sand towards the Dois Irmãos peaks.

card.hook: Even with no match on, the Maracanã is so big it makes you feel like a very small football. Its outline is about 588 m across, so you'll be hunting for ways to fit it on your screen.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, in front of the main entrance by the Bellini statue, and turn to face north-east before you start shooting. The statue in the foreground helps frame the main facade.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the sweep of the bowl from close up. Switch to 1x for a more natural view, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the roof edge and the stadium's name or signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roof edge up with a horizontal line so the stadium doesn't look like it's leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the stadium wall. Match and event days are much busier, so allow extra time.
card.selfie_here: Head for the Pelé statue on the forecourt and turn so the stadium is behind you. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) to fit more of the curve over your shoulder. Guides name the entrance statue differently (Pelé or Bellini), so check on the ground which one you're standing by.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the statue at the main entrance, where tour groups stop, and ask someone to frame you with the full entrance and pillars behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are not allowed at match-day entry to the stadium, so leave yours behind if you have a ticket. One guide says the floors can get slippery in rain on the tour, so skip the sandals. Check the official site before going inside.
card.challenge: Wait for a stranger to stroll through your wide shot, then snap it so they look tiny next to the stadium.
card.good_to_know: The Maracanã opened in 1950 for the World Cup. That's where Brazil lost 2-1 to Uruguay in the deciding match, a defeat Brazilians still call the Maracanazo. It holds 73,139 people today and is still Brazil's largest stadium. Its name comes from a Tupi word for a type of parrot, which makes a nice caption.

card.hook: Most people snap the Museum of Tomorrow from the busy street side and wonder why it looks cluttered. Walk round to the water and it turns into a long, low spaceship with a roof reaching out over the bay.
card.stand_here: Head for Praça Mauá first. The museum is to the north-east, about 5 minutes on foot. Then walk round to the bay side, by the reflecting pools and the water's edge, and face the museum so the sweeping roof and solar-panel facade fill the front of your shot, with the bay and the Rio-Niterói bridge behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole roof and its reflection in the pools. Switch to 1x for a more natural look with the bay behind, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out the solar panels and the bridge in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then drag the brightness down a little so the sky stays blue and the white structure doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun is setting and the light on the facade gets better. It's also a nice time to wander along the water and try a few spots.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the reflecting pool between the museum and the bay, next to Frank Stella's Puffed Star sculpture, if it's still there. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold your phone so the museum's sweeping shape curves behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Boulevard Olímpico side of the building, where the full cantilever shows over the water, to take your photo with the museum behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum doesn't allow selfie sticks, because they disturb other visitors, so use your arm. Flash isn't allowed either, and photos and video are fine everywhere except the Cosmos area, the first area of the main exhibition.
card.challenge: Take one photo with the roofline on the top third of your gridlines and its reflection in the water below. Then take another from ten steps further along, and spot how the building changes shape.
card.good_to_know: The Museum of Tomorrow (Museu do Amanhã) is a science museum designed by Santiago Calatrava. It opened on 17 December 2015 as part of the renewal of Rio's port area before the 2016 Olympics. Inside, the main exhibition moves through five themes: Cosmos, Earth, Anthropocene, Tomorrow and Us.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Praça Mauá first. The museum is to the north-east, about 5 minutes on foot. Then walk round to the bay side, by the reflecting pools and the water's edge, and face the museum so the sweeping roof and solar-panel facade fill the front of your shot, with the bay and the Rio-Niterói bridge behind.

card.hook: Imagine a staircase that looks like someone emptied a thousand postcards onto it. That's the Selarón Steps, and the colour is so strong you almost can't take a bad picture.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, at the bottom on the first flight by Rua Joaquim Silva. Face up the stairs so the tiled steps rise away from you and fill the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic view up the staircase. Higher up, try 2x or more (depends on your phone) to zoom in on single tiles.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the middle of the staircase up with the centre of the frame, and hold your phone low so the steps climb up the picture.
card.best_time: Go between 8 and 10 in the morning, when the staircase is almost empty. From late morning to late afternoon it gets busy, and weekends and Carnival are the busiest of all.
card.selfie_here: Head to the upper steps, turn right at the Brazilian flag, and pose with the tiles behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more colour, and keep the tiles over your shoulder. It's quieter up there than at the bottom, but check the upper steps on the map first.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the foot of the steps on the Lapa side and shoot upward while you stand on the lower steps, so the whole staircase rises behind you (step aside if people are queuing for the same shot).
card.rules_and_safety: The steps are uneven and slippery after rain, so watch your feet. Keep your phone secure when you're not shooting and your belongings close, because pickpocketing has been reported in the streets around here. If a local photographer offers a paid posed shot, agree the price first. Check the current policy on leaving tiles before you go.
card.challenge: Hunt down a hand-painted tile of a pregnant woman. There are around 300, so you've got good odds.
card.good_to_know: Chilean-born artist Jorge Selarón began renovating these worn steps outside his house in 1990, first with blue, green and yellow fragments, the colours of the Brazilian flag. Today there are 215 steps over about 125 metres, with more than 2000 tiles from over 60 countries. Many of the later tiles were donated by visitors.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, at the bottom on the first flight by Rua Joaquim Silva. Face up the stairs so the tiled steps rise away from you and fill the frame.

card.hook: Most people queue for the Christ-above-the-palms shot out front, but round the back of the mansion there are stone caves, little towers and pools tucked into the rainforest. It's calmer, a bit mysterious, and much easier to have to yourself.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of Parque Lage, then follow the paths round to the back of the mansion. The caves and pools are back there, so face a cave opening with the greenery beyond it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the caves, towers and pools, so you fit in plenty of rainforest and a sense of depth. Switch to 1x for a cleaner shot of one cave opening or tower, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for stonework and leaves.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, then tap a darker spot inside a cave and slide it brighter so the shade doesn't turn muddy.
card.best_time: Go when the light is soft, and try to avoid the busiest hours so the paths are yours. An overcast day actually helps under the trees because it softens the harsh patches of light. Flytographer suggests 8 am to 4 pm, and reviews say before 11 am keeps the queues down.
card.selfie_here: Head to the courtyard reflecting pool in front of the Palacete. Use the front camera at 0.5x and stand beside the water with the Christ the Redeemer statue over your shoulder, mirrored in the pool. If the pool queue is long, the Palacete terrace is a second angle on the building and the statue.

card.rules_and_safety: Reports say the Palacete is temporarily closed for restoration, so the courtyard pool spot may not be open. Check when you arrive, and check the official site for access to the mansion and courtyard.

card.good_to_know: Antonio Martins Lage bought the property in the early 1830s, and the rustic garden with its artificial grotto dates to around 1840. In the 1920s industrialist Henrique Lage had the mansion remodelled. Today it houses a visual arts school and a café that's open to the public.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of Parque Lage, then follow the paths round to the back of the mansion. The caves and pools are back there, so face a cave opening with the greenery beyond it.

card.hook: Picture a dirt path with tall palms marching away in two neat rows, and you standing in the middle looking very pleased with yourself. That's the Jardim Botânico's famous palm lane, and the symmetry does most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Aleia Barbosa Rodrigues at the entrance end of the lane, right in the middle of the path. Face straight down it, towards the far end.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the lane looks natural, with the trunks running off to the far end. Try 0.5x for the full height of the palms, but keep your phone level so the trunks don't lean. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) squeezes the palms together and makes the lane look longer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the far end of the lane on the centre line, then tap the far end and drag the slider to make it a touch darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the low sun throws long shadows down the path. By midday the light goes flat and the scene loses its drama.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of the Avenue of Royal Palms (Avenida das Palmeiras Imperiais) with the palm corridor behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to fit in the tall trunks. The Central Fountain by the pond is also a good selfie spot, with Christ the Redeemer visible in the distance behind you. Its exact position isn't given, so check the map.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a ticketed garden with set opening times, so check the official site before you go. Photos for personal use are generally fine. Skip the flash in sensitive areas and follow any posted signs.
card.challenge: Get a perfectly centred palm-lane shot with no strangers in it. Bonus points if a capuchin or marmoset photobombs you.
card.good_to_know: The Avenue of Royal Palms is 750 metres long and has 134 palms. They all descend from a single tree, the Palma Mater, which was destroyed by lightning long ago. The garden was founded in 1808 by King John VI of Portugal and opened to the public in 1822.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Aleia Barbosa Rodrigues at the entrance end of the lane, right in the middle of the path. Face straight down it, towards the far end.

card.hook: Picture a room lined with big crystal mirrors from Antwerp, rosewood trim and carved wooden furniture, and a stained-glass skylight waiting above your head. That's Confeitaria Colombo, and it's why people photograph a coffee break.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map sits right at Confeitaria Colombo, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Snap the outside first, then step just inside the entrance and face along the main hall.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole hall, mirrors and ceiling in one shot. Use 1x for tables, cakes and mirror frames, then zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the carved wood or the stained glass, so you don't have to lean over other people.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the mirrors and columns so the room looks nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go outside the busiest meal times, when there are fewer people in the room and it's easier to frame the interior without crowds.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the second-floor salon near the oval opening between the floors, where the staircase and stained-glass ceiling frame the room. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and let the historic interior fill the space behind your shoulder. Downstairs, you can also stand in front of the big mirror panels on the side walls with the grand staircase behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the pedestrian street in front of the facade at Rua Gonçalves Dias 32 and ask a passer-by to frame you with the whole front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working café, so be considerate of other customers, and check the official site for any photo rules before you go. One review says the area around the café isn't the safest, so keep an eye on your things and take care.
card.challenge: Find the oval opening, tilt your phone up and catch the stained-glass skylight, without your own reflection sneaking into a mirror.
card.good_to_know: Confeitaria Colombo opened in 1894, founded by Portuguese immigrants Joaquim Borges de Meireles and Manuel José Lebrão. Between 1912 and 1918 the halls got their Art Nouveau look, and a second-floor tearoom was added in 1922. Over the years it has welcomed Brazilian writers and artists, heads of state and Queen Elizabeth II.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map sits right at Confeitaria Colombo, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Snap the outside first, then step just inside the entrance and face along the main hall.

card.hook: Arpoador is the place in Rio where you can watch surfers ride left-hand waves right beside a pile of rocks, with a huge curve of beach behind them. Not bad for one phone screen.
card.stand_here: Stand at the overlook at the Arpoador end of Parque Garota de Ipanema, beside the beach, and face west along the sand. Arpoador's rocks lie a short way to the south, so you get them, the lifeguard post and the Ipanema and Leblon shoreline all in one view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the rocks, the beach and the sweep towards Leblon. Switch to 1x for a tidier frame, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out surfers or the lifeguard post.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and lay the curve of the beach along one of the lower lines, with the rocks off to one side.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is lovely, when the beach lights come on. Around midsummer the sun sets over the sea from here, which is unusual on this coast, and it gets busy, so arrive early to grab a spot.
card.selfie_here: Climb up to Pedra do Arpoador, the flat rock at the point between Ipanema and Copacabana. Stand on top, face left of the sunset line so the Dois Irmãos peaks are in the frame, and use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) with the scenery over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The rock is open to the public with walkways, but it can be slippery and big waves sometimes wash over it, so keep well back from the surf line. Strong currents and waves here are a genuine hazard, and it's not a casual swim beach.
card.challenge: Get a surfer, the lifeguard post and the curve of the beach into one shot, then see if you can spot them all again in your photo later.
card.good_to_know: Arpoador means "harpoon thrower", and it's a small rocky peninsula splitting Ipanema from Copacabana. The rocks create steady left-hand breakers that can reach 7 to 10 feet, which makes this one of Rio's best city surf spots. Part of the area belongs to Ipanema and part to Copacabana.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the overlook at the Arpoador end of Parque Garota de Ipanema, beside the beach, and face west along the sand. Arpoador's rocks lie a short way to the south, so you get them, the lifeguard post and the Ipanema and Leblon shoreline all in one view.

card.hook: Stand under a 90 m concrete arch with three legs and you'll feel small in the best way. The shapes here are big, simple and repeated, so even a quick snap looks planned.
card.stand_here: Stand in Praça da Apoteose, under the big concrete arch at the end of the avenue. From the square, the middle of the parade area is about 4 minutes on foot to the north, and the avenue runs away from you that way, so face north.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole arch and the stands into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched view of the avenue's end, or try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the legs of the arch against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the arch or the sky, then drag the slider to make it a touch darker so the concrete keeps its detail against a bright sky.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, early morning or late afternoon, when the light on the concrete is softer. Parade nights start at 8pm just before Lent, and that's when the avenue is at its liveliest.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, hold it low and slightly tilted up, and switch to 0.5x if your phone has it. Turn so the big arch sits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The avenue and grandstands are ticketed on parade nights, so check the official site before you go. One reviewer says Sector 9 is mostly for tourists, absolutely safe, and has good visibility. That's one person's opinion, not an official word.
card.challenge: Crouch a little, keep your phone level, and get the arch dead centre with the stands making perfect sides, with no wonky vertical lines allowed.
card.good_to_know: Oscar Niemeyer designed the Sambadrome. It was commissioned in 1983 and finished in 1984. The parade avenue is 700 m long, the whole venue holds about 90,000 people, and the arch has become a symbol of Carnival. Under the bleachers there's even a school with 115 classrooms.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Praça da Apoteose, under the big concrete arch at the end of the avenue. From the square, the middle of the parade area is about 4 minutes on foot to the north, and the avenue runs away from you that way, so face north.

selfie_research.safety: One reviewer says Sector 9 is mostly for tourists, absolutely safe, and has good visibility.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor can stand with the Sambadrome behind them for a selfie, or a spot where a passer-by can photograph the visitor with the whole landmark, so both fields are left empty rather than guessed. The closest documented vantage is the top of Sector 9 (grandstand), which Wikipedia describes as a panoramic shot of the parade with the arch visible; this is a view of the parade, not a selfie spot, and it is inside the grandstand, which may only be open on event days. Tripadvisor forum users recommend monopods over tripods for the frisa boxes, and Airial says you may need a tripod for sharp night shots, but neither page states an official rule about tripods or selfie sticks, so no rules are reported. The Wanderlog reviewer mentions a photo-op with a replica football trophy, but the page does not say where it is, so it cannot be mapped. The Sambadrome is at R. Marquês de Sapucaí, s/n, Cidade Nova, and Wikipedia lists Santo Cristo as the location. A search for a Sambadrome-specific selfie or photo point (for example, at the entrance or the Praça Onze end) and a check on Google Maps or a local guide would be the next step. The safety remark comes from one reviewer's opinion, not an official source.

card.hook: Picture a church with no spire, no bell tower and no pointy bits, just a huge concrete cone sitting in the middle of Rio. It's a surprise the first time you see it, and it's easy to spot from far away.
card.stand_here: Stand in Praça da Cruz Vermelha, the open square that gives you enough room to fit the whole cone in one shot. The cathedral lies to the east, about 10 minutes on foot, so walk towards the cone and face it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to take in the whole cone with a little sky above it. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter, cleaner shape. Only use 0.5x if you move closer and need to fit the full height in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the cone up with the centre of the frame and keep your phone level so the sides don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the building than harsh midday sun. If the sky is very bright, tap the cathedral and slide it a touch darker so the walls keep their detail.
card.selfie_here: In Praça da Cruz Vermelha, use the front camera with the cathedral's exterior behind you, and step back so the whole cone fits over your shoulder. For a livelier shot, try Pedra do Sal in the city centre in the evening, when the area comes alive with music and dancing, with the cathedral in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open to everyone, but the cathedral is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside. Photos are allowed without flash, and be mindful during services. One guide told a group to take their phones out only for the photo and put them away straight after, so it's wise to do the same.
card.challenge: Get the cone perfectly centred, gridlines lined up and sides straight, then see if you can take a selfie with its tip sitting right above your head like a party hat.
card.good_to_know: The cathedral was designed by Edgar de Oliveira da Fonseca in a modern style inspired by Mayan pyramids, and it was built between 1964 and 1979. It's about 75 metres high and about 106 metres across on the outside. It's dedicated to Saint Sebastian, the patron saint of Rio de Janeiro.

card.hook: Picture 42 white stone arches marching across Lapa, with a little tram rattling along the top like it owns the place. That's the Carioca Aqueduct, which everyone here calls Arcos da Lapa.
card.stand_here: Stand on Rua do Lavradio and face north-east. The arches sit that way, seen at an angle along the street rather than straight on.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze more of that long row into the frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out the pattern of the top arches or a tram crossing.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the arches, then slide it a little darker so the white stone keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early or around dusk. The tram only crosses now and then, so check the timing if you want it in your picture.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement directly beneath the arches, where the tram deck shows above you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and turn so the arches are behind your shoulder. It's the nearest spot to a true selfie position, so check it on the ground.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to shoot from the open side of Praça Cardeal Câmara, facing the arcade, so the full double row of arches fits in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Avoid the area alone at night. One visitor review also warned about robberies near the arches, and advised going in daytime with a guide.
card.challenge: Line up the tops of the arches with a gridline, then wait for the tram to cross and see if you can catch it.
card.good_to_know: The aqueduct was inaugurated in 1750 to bring fresh water from the Carioca River into the city. The stretch between the Santa Teresa and Santo Antônio hills is about 270 metres long, with 42 arches on two storeys, up to 17.6 metres high. Since 1896 the top level has carried the Santa Teresa tram.

card.hook: Rio has beaches and a giant statue, yet plenty of locals will tell you the real heart of the city is a lake with a bike path around it. Walk to the water's edge here and you'll see why: flat water, a big green hill and a lot of sky.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parque dos Patins, the shaded park on the lakeside shore. The lagoon lies about 432 m to the east of that point, so face the water, with the Corcovado hill rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the water, the hill and a big sky all in one shot. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring Corcovado closer so it looms over the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, then tap the sky and slide it a little darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon and stay into sunset, when the sun drops behind the hills and the light turns soft. Midday looks flat and hot, so save that time for a snack at the kiosks.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with the water behind you, climb to Mirante do Sacopã, the lookout at the top of the Parque da Catacumba trail on the lagoon's eastern edge, and turn your back to the view. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the lagoon and the ocean sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The trail up to Mirante do Sacopã is short but steep, so allow for a demanding climb. Swimming in the lagoon is not recommended, and it's worth checking the official site before you go in case of local changes or restrictions at Parque dos Patins.
card.challenge: Can you get three neat stripes in one photo: water at the bottom, hill in the middle and a good slice of sky on top, with the horizon dead level?
card.good_to_know: The lagoon is nicknamed "the Heart of Rio de Janeiro". The water covers about 2.4 million square metres, and the paved path around it is about 7.5 kilometres long. The name comes from Rodrigo de Freitas de Carvalho, who married into the landowning Fagundes family in 1702, and at Christmas a huge tree on a floating platform moves around the lagoon.

card.hook: Picture the whole curve of Copacabana Beach laid out in one frame, with Sugarloaf sitting at the far end like it was placed there on purpose. That's the view from the top of an old army fort.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject: the upper parapet and gun-turret area inside Forte de Copacabana. Face north along the beach, back toward Leme, with Sugarloaf Mountain behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the full sweep of the beach from the parapet. Switch to 1x for the turrets and walls, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull Sugarloaf closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sea or the sky, then drag the slider to make it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour and the beach doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is lovely for the light on Sugarloaf. Go early in the morning, or on a weekday, if you want fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Pose beside the big 305 mm cannons on the seaward side, with the grey turret as your historic backdrop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the cannon over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of the fort's outer gate off Avenida Atlântica and ask a passer-by on the sidewalk to photograph you with the gate and walls behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The fort is a working army site, so bring photo ID and expect an ID check at the gate. Photos inside the Army museum weren't allowed according to an older marker, so keep your shooting outdoors and check for any current photo rules. Take your shot, then put your phone away before you move.
card.challenge: Can you get a grey gun turret in one corner and Sugarloaf in the distance in the same shot, with the beach curving between them?
card.good_to_know: The army began building the fort in 1908 and finished it in 1914. Its two armoured turrets, one with a pair of 305 mm guns and one with a pair of 190 mm guns, are among the last heavy cupolas of their kind in the world. The fort was the centre of a short army revolt in 1922, stopped being a coastal artillery post in 1987, and now houses the Army Historical Museum. It was also a venue for the 2016 Olympics.

card.hook: Picture a jogger and a cyclist zipping past while Sugarloaf Mountain rises over a huge, calm bay. That's Flamengo Park, and the postcard view is only a short walk from the greenery.
card.stand_here: Stand on Praia do Flamengo, at the western end of the beach. Face out across the bay so Sugarloaf rises ahead of you, with the sand and the palm-lined promenade in front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the full postcard of beach, promenade and Sugarloaf. Try 0.5x to get more palms and promenade in the foreground, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring Sugarloaf closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, so both the bay and the sky get some room.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is softer and the crowds are thinner.
card.selfie_here: Try the sand at the southern end of Praia do Flamengo, close to Marina da Glória, where a guide recommends an unobstructed Sugarloaf view. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep Sugarloaf over your shoulder. The park's greenery should be behind you too.
card.rules_and_safety: The park and beach are open public space with no restrictions reported, but check the official site before you go in case of events or closures.
card.challenge: Catch a jogger or cyclist whizzing through the foreground with Sugarloaf waiting calmly behind them.
card.good_to_know: Flamengo Park (also called Aterro do Flamengo) covers about 120 hectares and was finished in 1965. Lota de Macedo Soares first imagined it, Affonso Eduardo Reidy designed it, and Roberto Burle Marx laid out the gardens. Inside you'll find the Museum of Modern Art, the Carmen Miranda Museum and the World War II memorial.

card.hook: Picture 9 January 1822: Pedro I steps onto a balcony here, looks out over the square and announces he's staying in Brazil. You can stand in that same square today and photograph the whole building.
card.stand_here: Stand in Praça XV de Novembro, right in front of the facade, and face the palace across the square. Step back until the whole long front fits.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic shot of the whole front. If the square is busy or you're too close, tap 0.5x. For the marble doorway, the balconies and the rows of windows, go to 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. One guide describes the light then as soft and warm on the building.
card.selfie_here: Head into the small inner courtyard, next to the bistro. A visitor guide calls it a peaceful photo spot, with the building's architecture and greenery as your backdrop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the scene, and hold the phone slightly above eye level.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the square on the Rua Primeiro de Março side, near the Carmo church, while you stand in front of the facade, so they can frame you with the palace behind.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally allowed inside, but video may be restricted in some areas or for specific exhibitions. One visitor review advises caution when walking around Praça XV. The palace and cultural centre may have their own visiting rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the row of balconies at 2x, then strike your best 'I'm staying!' pose for a friend to snap.
card.good_to_know: The Paço Imperial was finished in 1743 in a plain Baroque style as the home of the colonial governors. It became a royal palace in 1808, and in 1888 Princess Isabel signed the Lei Áurea, which ended slavery, in one of its rooms. After years as a post office, a big restoration in 1980 brought back its look from around 1818, and it has been a cultural centre since 1984.

card.hook: Picture an opera house dropped into the middle of a wide-open square, with the names of famous artists carved right into its outer walls. That's the Theatro Municipal, and the square gives you room to take it all in.
card.stand_here: Stand in Praça Marechal Floriano, the Cinelândia square in Centro. The theatre is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot. Face the main front across the square and keep your phone level.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front and the square into one frame, then try 1x for a more natural look. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the central sculpture group and the carved names.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day is kinder to the front than harsh midday sun. Go when the square is quieter if you want fewer people in your frame.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the square, facing the front of the theatre so the building fills the frame behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x if your phone has it. If you take a guided tour, the wide marble staircase inside is another good selfie spot, with the carved balustrade and bronze lamps behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of the square from the front of the building so the whole façade fits, while you stand in front of the theatre.
card.rules_and_safety: On guided tours flash isn't allowed, and photography is barred during performances. This comes from one source that may be out of date, so check with the theatre before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 5x and find one of the artists' names carved on the outer walls, then get a clear shot of it.
card.good_to_know: The theatre is modelled on the Paris Opéra of Charles Garnier. Building began in 1905 on a foundation of 1,180 wood poles, and it opened on 14 July 1909. Today it seats 2,361 and mostly stages ballet and classical music.

card.hook: Picture a whitewashed front with dark granite picked out around every window, door and column. It looks like someone drew it with a thick pen, and it makes Candelária Church an easy, graphic photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Praça Pio X, the open square in front of the church's main facade. From here the church is to the south-west, so face that way and you'll see the bell towers and dome above the front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from across the square to fit the whole facade. If you can't step back far enough, tap 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the towers, dome and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the church's vertical edges with them, and keep your phone level so the towers don't lean inward.
card.best_time: Daytime is best for the full facade, with sky above and space around the building. In the evening the church is floodlit, so try night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the area near the Pira Olímpica (the Olympic flame monument) nearby. One reviewer called the view of the church from there beautiful, though it isn't officially a selfie spot. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x, and keep the church over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand well back on Praça Pio X, facing the main facade, while you stand in front of the church so the whole building fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open public space, but the church is a place of worship and may have set visiting times, so check the official site before you go inside.
card.challenge: Get the whole facade, both towers and the dome in one frame with the gridlines lined up. Then take a floodlit version after dark and compare.
card.good_to_know: The main facade was built between 1775 and 1811 in Portuguese colonial Baroque style, with some neoclassical touches like the flat front and triangular pediment. The dome was finished in 1877. It was made in white Lioz stone in Lisbon and shipped to Brazil, and when it was completed it was the tallest structure in the city.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Praça Pio X, the open square in front of the church's main facade. From here the church is to the south-west, so face that way and you'll see the bell towers and dome above the front.
